questions.q: Over how many full crankshaft revolutions is one four-stroke Otto cycle completed for each cylinder?
options: Three
Four
One
Two
questions.explain: The four strokes - intake, compression, power and exhaust - are completed over two full crankshaft revolutions per cylinder.
questions.src: completed over two full crankshaft revolutions per cylinder

questions.q: Which list gives the four strokes of the Otto cycle in the correct order?
options: Power, exhaust, intake, compression
Intake, power, compression, exhaust
Intake, compression, power, exhaust
Compression, intake, exhaust, power
questions.explain: The charge is drawn in (intake), compressed, ignited so the expanding gas drives the piston (power), and finally expelled (exhaust).
questions.src: intake, compression, power and exhaust

questions.q: How does the manual define detonation?
options: Uncontrolled, spontaneous ignition of the end-gas ahead of the flame front
The orderly spread of the flame front across the charge after spark ignition
Ignition of the charge by the spark plug later than the timing map intended
Burning of lubricating oil that has seeped past the piston rings into the cylinder
questions.explain: Detonation is uncontrolled, spontaneous ignition of the end-gas ahead of the flame front. Raising compression ratio too far invites it before the knock sensor and ignition retard can intervene.
questions.src: uncontrolled, spontaneous ignition of the end-gas ahead of the flame front

questions.q: Raising the compression ratio improves thermal efficiency, but raising it too far invites detonation.
options: True
False
questions.explain: A higher ratio extracts more work from the same charge, so thermal efficiency rises - but too high a ratio risks detonation.
questions.src: raising it too far invites detonation

questions.q: How does a diesel engine ignite its fuel?
options: By a heated throttle plate that raises the temperature of the incoming air
By compression alone, injecting fuel into air already hot enough to auto-ignite it
By a spark plug fired from a three-dimensional speed and load map
By pre-mixing fuel and air upstream of the intake valve and igniting it with a coil
questions.explain: Diesels share the same four strokes but ignite by compression alone. There is no spark event and no throttle plate.
questions.src: ignite by compression alone

questions.q: Why does a diesel's efficiency hold up far better than a petrol engine's at partial load?
options: It runs at a lower compression ratio than a petrol engine
It uses a much larger spark advance than a petrol engine at light load
Power is regulated by fuel quantity rather than by a throttle plate
It pre-mixes the charge more thoroughly than a petrol engine does
questions.explain: With no throttle plate, a diesel controls power by the quantity of fuel injected, so it avoids a petrol engine's partial-load losses.
questions.src: power is instead regulated by the quantity of fuel injected

questions.q: What is the typical output range of the Mass Air Flow (MAF) sensor?
options: 2 grams per second at idle to 95 grams per second at full load
0.5 grams per second at idle to 20 grams per second at full load
12 grams per second at idle to 200 grams per second at full load
30 grams per second at idle to 101 grams per second at full load
questions.explain: MAF output runs from about 2 g/s at idle to 95 g/s at full load. (30 kPa to 101 kPa is the MAP sensor's pressure range.)
questions.src: 2 grams per second at idle to 95 grams per second at full load

questions.q: What common-rail pressure does the high-pressure fuel pump produce on direct-injection petrol engines?
options: 1800 bar or more
Between 350 kPa and 400 kPa
Between 5 bar and 20 bar
Between 50 bar and 200 bar
questions.explain: Direct-injection petrol engines run 50-200 bar; modern common-rail diesels reach 1800 bar or more. (350-400 kPa is the low-pressure idle rail check in section 3.)
questions.src: between 50 bar and 200 bar on direct-injection petrol engines

t0006.title: Ch 1 - 2. ECU CONTROL STRATEGY & SENSOR INPUTS

questions.q: During which condition does the ECU use open-loop fuel control?
options: Cold start, wide open throttle, or an oxygen sensor signal that is not yet valid
Steady cruise once the engine is fully warm and the oxygen sensor is active
Idle with the engine warm and the oxygen sensor reporting the mixture
Any time the long-term fuel trim has drifted beyond plus 25 percent
questions.explain: Open-loop meters fuel from the stored base map with no feedback. Closed-loop is used for normal warmed-up running.
questions.src: used during cold start, wide open throttle

questions.q: What air-fuel ratio does the ECU hold in closed-loop operation?
options: A deliberately rich ratio of 12.5 to 1
A fixed ratio of 10 to 1 at all loads
A deliberately lean ratio of 17.2 to 1
The stoichiometric ratio of 14.7 to 1
questions.explain: The upstream oxygen sensor reports the actual mixture and the ECU trims injector pulse width to hold 14.7 to 1.
questions.src: stoichiometric target of 14.7 to 1

questions.q: A long-term fuel trim beyond which value indicates a fault requiring investigation?
options: Plus 5 percent
Plus 10 percent
Plus 25 percent
Minus 10 percent
questions.explain: Long-term trim accumulates the running average (injector wear, air leaks, fuel quality); beyond +25 percent is a fault. Short-term trim normally swings about +/-10 percent.
questions.src: a long-term trim beyond plus 25 percent indicates a fault requiring investigation

questions.q: Between what values does short-term fuel trim typically oscillate?
options: Minus 2 percent and plus 2 percent
Minus 10 percent and plus 10 percent
Minus 25 percent and plus 25 percent
Zero and plus 5 percent
questions.explain: Short-term trim responds within milliseconds and typically oscillates between minus 10 and plus 10 percent.
questions.src: typically oscillates between minus 10 percent and plus 10 percent

questions.q: How does the MAP sensor arrive at the mass of air entering the cylinder?
options: It counts injector pulses per crankshaft revolution at the current load
It measures it directly with a heated wire placed in the intake tract
It infers it from manifold pressure, engine speed and volumetric efficiency
It reads the oxygen content of the exhaust and works backwards from it
questions.explain: MAF measures air mass directly in the intake tract; MAP infers it by the speed-density method. Running both lets the ECU cross-check one against the other.
questions.src: while MAP infers it from manifold pressure, engine speed and known volumetric efficiency

questions.q: A MAF reading that drifts away from the MAP-derived estimate is an early, pre-DTC indicator of what?
options: An over-pressurised fuel rail or a stuck injector
A vacuum leak or a contaminated sensor element
A worn timing belt or a stretched camshaft chain
A failed knock sensor or a retarded ignition map
questions.explain: Because the two sensors measure the same quantity by different routes, a disagreement flags a vacuum leak or contamination before a DTC sets.
questions.src: early, pre-DTC indicator of a vacuum leak or a contaminated sensor element

questions.q: In what size steps is ignition advance typically retarded when the knock sensor detects detonation?
options: 1 degree at a time
10 degrees at a time
5 degrees at a time
2 degrees at a time
questions.explain: Advance is retarded in steps of about 2 degrees until knock ceases.
questions.src: typically in steps of 2 degrees until knock ceases

questions.q: Why is ignition advance retarded during warm-up?
options: To raise exhaust gas temperature and accelerate catalyst light-off
To reduce intake manifold vacuum so the idle speed stays stable
To protect the oxygen sensor element from thermal shock during warm-up
To keep the injectors cool while the coolant is still cold
questions.explain: Retarded timing makes the exhaust hotter, so the catalyst reaches light-off sooner (see the Exhaust & Emissions chapter).
questions.src: to raise exhaust gas temperature and accelerate catalyst light-off

questions.q: Before the fuel rail pressure check, the engine must cool below what temperature?
options: 40 degrees Celsius
60 degrees Celsius
20 degrees Celsius
80 degrees Celsius
questions.explain: Depressurise the fuel system and let the engine cool below 40 degrees Celsius before beginning.
questions.src: allow the engine to cool below 40 degrees Celsius

questions.q: What idle speed is used while recording the fuel rail pressure?
options: 3000 RPM
1500 RPM
750 RPM
2000 RPM
questions.explain: Idle the engine at 750 RPM and record the pressure. 3000 RPM is the later step used to confirm pressure rises without instability.
questions.src: idle at 750 RPM

questions.q: What is the specified idle fuel rail pressure range?
options: 450 kPa to 500 kPa
200 kPa to 250 kPa
600 kPa to 700 kPa
350 kPa to 400 kPa
questions.explain: The reading must fall within the specified idle range of 350 kPa to 400 kPa.
questions.src: idle range of 350 kPa to 400 kPa

questions.q: With the engine stopped, what must the fuel rail hold, and for how long?
options: At least 350 kPa after 1 minute
At least 250 kPa after 10 minutes
At least 100 kPa after 30 minutes
At least 400 kPa after 5 minutes
questions.explain: The rail must hold at least 250 kPa after 10 minutes.
questions.src: holds at least 250 kPa after 10 minutes

questions.q: A rail pressure that decays faster than specified after shut-down indicates what?
options: A contaminated MAF element or a weak knock sensor
A leaking exhaust manifold or a worn spark plug
A blocked fuel filter or a weak fuel pump
A leaking injector or a failed check valve
questions.explain: A faster decay means fuel is bleeding out of the rail - through a leaking injector or a failed check valve.
questions.src: A faster decay indicates a leaking injector or a failed check valve

questions.q: What is the nominal injector coil resistance specification?
options: 12 ohms plus or minus 0.6 ohms at 20 degrees Celsius
12 ohms plus or minus 1.2 ohms at 20 degrees Celsius
120 ohms plus or minus 6 ohms at 20 degrees Celsius
1.2 ohms plus or minus 0.06 ohms at 20 degrees Celsius
questions.explain: Nominal injector resistance is 12 ohms +/- 0.6 ohms at 20 degrees Celsius, measured on the 200 ohm range.
questions.src: 12 ohms plus or minus 0.6 ohms at 20 degrees Celsius

questions.q: Resistance across all injectors must be matched within what value, even if each is individually in specification?
options: 0.1 ohm
1 ohm
10 ohms
5 ohms
questions.explain: A mismatch produces uneven cylinder fuelling even where every injector is individually within specification.
questions.src: matched within 1 ohm

questions.q: What is the tightening torque for the fuel rail mounting bolts?
options: 10 newton metres
20 newton metres
22 newton metres
28 newton metres
questions.explain: Fuel rail mounting bolts: 22 N-m, in a diagonal sequence. (28 N-m is the pump bolts, 10 N-m the injector clamps, 20 N-m the knock sensor.)
questions.src: Fuel rail mounting bolts | 22 newton metres

questions.q: Which engine-management fastener requires a new sealing washer when it is refitted?
options: Injector clamp bolts
Fuel rail mounting bolts
Knock sensor mounting bolt
High-pressure pump retaining bolts
questions.explain: Injector clamp bolts (10 N-m) - replace the sealing washer.
questions.src: Injector clamp bolts | 10 newton metres | Replace sealing washer

questions.q: Which principle states that pressure applied anywhere in an enclosed, incompressible fluid is transmitted equally in every direction?
options: Newton's third law
Pascal's law
Bernoulli's principle
Boyle's law
questions.explain: Every hydraulic brake circuit works from Pascal's law.
questions.src: Pascal's law

questions.q: What two multiplications turn the driver's foot force into caliper clamping force?
options: The tyre contact patch area, then the coefficient of road friction
The reluctor ring tooth count, then the sensor air gap setting
The pedal's lever ratio, then the master cylinder-to-caliper piston area ratio
The servo's vacuum level, then the ABS valve cycling rate per second
questions.explain: Foot force is multiplied by the pedal lever ratio and again by the area ratio between the master cylinder piston and each caliper piston.
questions.src: multiplied first by the pedal's lever ratio and again by the master cylinder's piston area

questions.q: Where does the ABS sit relative to the base hydraulic brake circuit?
options: Downstream of it, modulating pressure wheel by wheel
Inside each caliper, replacing the piston seals
In parallel to it, active only while the ignition is off
Upstream of the pedal, replacing the master cylinder
questions.explain: ABS sits downstream of the hydraulic circuit and modulates it wheel by wheel whenever a wheel is about to lock.
questions.src: sits downstream of that hydraulic circuit and modulates it, wheel by wheel

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed among the components of the ABS in the introduction?
options: ABS warning indicator lamp
Hydraulic Control Unit (HCU)
Wheel speed sensors
Vacuum servo (booster)
questions.explain: The introduction lists wheel speed sensors, the HCU, the ABS ECU, brake lines and solenoid valves, and the warning lamp. The vacuum servo belongs to the base hydraulic braking assembly.
questions.src: ABS Warning Indicator Lamp

questions.q: The ABS modulates brake pressure at a wheel only when that wheel is about to lock.
options: True
False
questions.explain: ABS modulates the circuit wheel by wheel whenever a wheel is about to lock.
questions.src: whenever a wheel is about to lock

questions.q: What class of lever is the brake pedal?
options: Class 3 - the effort is applied between the pivot and the load
Class 4 - a compound lever with a pivot at each end
Class 1 - the pivot sits between the load and the effort
Class 2 - the load sits between the pivot and the effort
questions.explain: The brake pedal is a Class 2 lever: the pivot is above the pedal pad and the push rod picks up the load between the pivot and the pad.
questions.src: The brake pedal is a Class 2 lever

questions.q: With a pedal lever ratio of 4 to 1, 200 newtons at the pedal pad becomes how much force at the push rod (before the servo adds anything)?
options: 1600 newtons
800 newtons
400 newtons
50 newtons
questions.explain: 200 N x 4 = 800 N at the push rod.
questions.src: 200 newtons at the pedal pad becomes 800 newtons at the push rod

questions.q: What sets the pedal's mechanical advantage?
options: The diameter of the brake lines to the calipers
The vacuum available at the servo's diaphragm
Where along the pedal arm the push rod connects
The number of pistons in each caliper bore
questions.explain: The mechanical advantage is set purely by where along the pedal arm the push rod connects.
questions.src: set purely by where along the pedal arm the push rod connects

questions.q: What produces the boost force in the vacuum servo?
options: Manifold vacuum on one side of its diaphragm, atmospheric pressure on the other
A belt-driven hydraulic pump that pressurises fluid behind the push rod
An electric motor inside the HCU that drives the push rod forward
Compressed nitrogen released from the accumulator on each stroke
questions.explain: Pressing the pedal admits atmospheric pressure to the rear chamber only; the pressure difference pushes the push rod forward with several times the driver's force.
questions.src: pressure difference between engine manifold vacuum on one side of its diaphragm and atmospheric pressure on the other

questions.q: What happens if the servo loses vacuum sealing, for example through a cracked hose or failed one-way check valve?
options: The pedal becomes noticeably lighter and travels less than before
The brakes fail completely until the vacuum hose is repaired
Braking still works, but the pedal is harder and travels further
The ABS warning lamp is the only symptom; pedal feel is unchanged
questions.explain: Braking still works without boost, but the pedal is harder and travels further for the same deceleration.
questions.src: still stops the car, but the pedal becomes noticeably harder and travels further

questions.q: How are the master cylinder's two hydraulic circuits split?
options: By axle - the front brakes on one circuit, the rear brakes on the other
Primary circuit to all four wheels, secondary circuit as a spare
By side - the left wheels on one circuit, the right wheels on the other
Diagonally - one front and the opposite rear wheel per circuit
questions.explain: The diagonal split means a single leak anywhere still leaves one full circuit - and meaningful braking - in service.
questions.src: split diagonally (one front and the opposite rear wheel per circuit)

questions.q: If one hydraulic circuit leaks, the other circuit still provides meaningful braking.
options: True
False
questions.explain: The two pistons feed independent circuits, so a single leak still leaves one full circuit in service.
questions.src: a single leak anywhere in the system still leaves one full circuit

questions.q: How does the fluid reservoir feed the master cylinder piston chambers?
options: By gravity, through the compensating ports, with the pedal released
By vacuum drawn through the servo each time the pedal is released
By the HCU return pump, which refills the bore after every stop
By an electric pump that runs whenever the ignition is switched on
questions.explain: The reservoir sits above the bore and gravity-feeds both chambers through their compensating ports whenever the pedal is fully released.
questions.src: gravity-feeds both piston chambers through their compensating ports

t0019.title: Ch 2 - 3. ABS HYDRAULIC CONTROL UNIT & WHEEL SPEED SENSORS

questions.q: What does each wheel speed sensor read in order to measure wheel speed?
options: The brake disc surface temperature
A painted stripe on the tyre sidewall
The caliper piston position
A toothed reluctor ring
questions.explain: Each sensor monitors its own wheel by reading a toothed reluctor ring and reports to the ABS ECU.
questions.src: reading a toothed reluctor ring

questions.q: Primary brake lines delivering master cylinder pressure to the HCU are rated for up to what pressure?
options: 1800 bar
314 bar
19 bar
200 bar
questions.explain: The primary brake lines are rated to withstand up to 314 bar.
questions.src: rated to withstand up to 314 bar

questions.q: At what rate does the HCU modulate pressure during an ABS event?
options: Up to 19 pulses per second
Up to 50 pulses per second
Up to 3 pulses per second
Up to 314 pulses per second
questions.explain: The HCU cycles at up to 19 pulses per second.
questions.src: up to 19 pulses per second

questions.q: What is the HCU together with the ABS ECU called?
options: The Hydraulic Modulator Assembly (HMA)
The Brake Control Cluster (BCC)
The Integrated Braking System (IBS)
The Anti-Lock Control Module (ACM)
questions.explain: The HCU houses the ABS ECU; together they form the Integrated Braking System, mounted on brackets with vibration-isolation bushes.
questions.src: called the Integrated Braking System (IBS)

questions.q: Into which two phases is HCU operation divided?
options: Pressure Build Phase, and Pressure Hold-and-Bleed Phase
Pressure Hold Phase, and Pressure Release & Reapply Phase
Inlet Valve Phase, and Outlet Valve Phase, in sequence
Wheel Lock Detection Phase, and Pump Priming Phase
questions.explain: HCU operation is explained as a pressure hold phase and a pressure release and reapply phase.
questions.src: Pressure Release & Reapply Phase

questions.q: What is 'cadence pulsing'?
options: A self-test sequence run through the valves at ignition on
A fault in which warped brake discs make the pedal vibrate
The vacuum servo cycling on and off while the engine idles
The hold-release-reapply cycle of the ABS, felt as pedal pulsation
questions.explain: Cadence pulsing is the rapid hold, release and reapply cycle commanded by the ABS ECU, felt through the pedal.
questions.src: known as cadence pulsing

questions.q: Pulsation through the brake pedal during an ABS event indicates a fault in the system.
options: True
False
questions.explain: Pedal pulsation is a normal indication that ABS is active, not a fault.
questions.src: this pedal feedback is a normal indication that ABS is active, not a fault

questions.q: What is the primary safety benefit ABS provides over a non-modulated brake system?
options: Steering control is retained because grip is kept at all four wheels
It lets the driver brake harder without any pedal pulsation
It removes the need for a conventional hydraulic back-up circuit
It always shortens stopping distance on every road surface
questions.explain: Keeping each wheel just below lock-up retains lateral grip at all four contact patches, so the driver can still steer.
questions.src: which is the primary safety benefit ABS provides

questions.q: When does the ABS ECU run its self-test sequence?
options: Once a month at the garage
At every ignition cycle
Only during hard braking
Only after the warning lamp has lit
questions.explain: It self-tests at every ignition cycle and continuously monitors sensor and valve circuit integrity.
questions.src: performs a self-test sequence at every ignition cycle

questions.q: What happens to braking if the ABS ECU or HCU fails?
options: Normal hydraulic braking continues at full force, without ABS modulation
The vehicle enters limp mode with braking limited to half force
Braking is disabled until the ignition is cycled and the ECU resets
Only the front circuit stays active until the unit is repaired
questions.explain: A back-up, non-ABS braking mode is retained at all times.
questions.src: the conventional hydraulic circuit continues to provide full braking force

questions.q: Which bleed nipple does the manual's bleeding procedure start with?
options: Always the front-left nipple first
Any nipple - the order does not matter
The one farthest from the master cylinder
The one nearest to the master cylinder
questions.explain: Connect the clear hose to the nipple farthest from the master cylinder, then repeat at each wheel in the specified sequence.
questions.src: bleed nipple farthest from the master cylinder

questions.q: Why is a diagnostic-tool HCU-cycle bleed sequence needed after a manual bleed?
options: It resets the pedal lever ratio held in the ABS ECU memory
It recalibrates the wheel speed sensors after the fluid change
It refills the reservoir automatically while the engine runs
A manual wheel bleed cannot reach air trapped inside the HCU itself
questions.explain: Commanding the HCU to cycle each solenoid purges air trapped inside the unit.
questions.src: a manual wheel bleed alone cannot reach this trapped air

questions.q: Where must the reservoir level be kept while bleeding?
options: Above the minimum mark throughout
Empty until the last wheel
Below the minimum mark to avoid overflow
Exactly at the maximum mark
questions.explain: Top up the reservoir and keep it above the minimum mark throughout.
questions.src: keep it above the minimum mark throughout

questions.q: What brake fluid is recommended, and how often is it replaced?
options: DOT 3, replaced every 12 months
DOT 4, replaced every 60 months
DOT 5, replaced every 48 months
DOT 4, replaced every 24 months
questions.explain: Recommended fluid is DOT 4, replaced every 24 months.
questions.src: DOT 4, replaced every 24 months

questions.q: What is the specified wheel speed sensor air gap?
options: 0.05 mm to 0.12 mm
0.5 mm to 1.2 mm
5 mm to 12 mm
2.5 mm to 3.0 mm
questions.explain: The air gap between sensor and reluctor ring is 0.5 mm to 1.2 mm.
questions.src: 0.5 mm to 1.2 mm

questions.q: In a rack-and-pinion system, what connects each end of the rack to a steering knuckle?
options: An anti-roll link
A strut bracket
A tie rod
A drive shaft
questions.explain: Rotating the pinion moves the rack sideways, and its ends connect through tie rods directly to each steering knuckle.
questions.src: the rack's own ends connect through tie rods directly to each steering knuckle

questions.q: On a variable-ratio rack, where are the teeth cut progressively finer for quicker response?
options: Toward the rack's centre, near straight-ahead
Evenly along the whole length of the rack
Toward the rack's outer ends, near full lock
Only on the pinion, never on the rack
questions.explain: Finer teeth toward the centre give quicker response near the straight-ahead position.
questions.src: teeth that are cut progressively finer toward the rack's centre

questions.q: What does Electric Power Steering (EPS) use in place of the pump, hoses and hydraulic fluid?
options: A belt-driven compressor and an air reservoir
An electric motor and a control module
A gas-charged accumulator feeding the rack
A vacuum servo acting on the steering column
questions.explain: EPS replaces the pump, hoses and fluid entirely with an electric motor on the column or rack, driven by a dedicated control module.
questions.src: replaces the pump, hoses and fluid entirely with an electric motor

questions.q: Which of these is an advantage of EPS named in the manual?
options: Higher fluid pressure at idle
A larger steering lock angle
Self-bleeding hydraulics
Speed-variable assist
questions.explain: Removing the engine-driven parasitic load also enables speed-variable assist and lane-keeping torque overlay.
questions.src: enabling speed-variable assist and lane-keeping torque overlay

questions.q: In hydraulic power steering, what does the rotary valve use to proportion the assistance?
options: The torque sensed at the input shaft
The distance the rack has travelled
The coolant temperature of the engine
The road speed of the vehicle
questions.explain: The rotary valve directs fluid to either side of the assist piston in proportion to the torque sensed at the input shaft.
questions.src: in proportion to torque sensed at the input shaft

questions.q: Which of these is one of the system components listed in the introduction?
options: Wheel Speed Sensor and Reluctor Ring
Torque Converter and Stator Assembly
Strut Support Bracket Assembly
Anti-Roll Bar and Drop Link Assembly
questions.explain: The list is the steering gear, suspension strut assembly, tie rod and drive shaft, and strut support bracket assembly.
questions.src: Strut Support Bracket Assembly

t0029.title: Ch 3 - 2. STEERING GEOMETRY & THE ACKERMANN PRINCIPLE

questions.q: When turning, which front wheel must be steered through the larger angle?
options: The outer wheel, because it has further to travel
Neither wheel - the rear axle sets the turn angle
Both wheels equally, to keep the arcs matched
The inner wheel, as it follows a smaller-radius arc
questions.explain: The inner wheel follows a smaller-radius arc, so it must be steered through a larger angle for every wheel to roll without scrubbing.
questions.src: it must be steered through a larger angle

questions.q: Equal steer angles at both front wheels would force one of them to scrub sideways through a turn.
options: True
False
questions.explain: That is why the inner wheel needs more angle than the outer wheel.
questions.src: equal steer angles at both front wheels would force one of them to scrub sideways

questions.q: Where do the axes of all wheels ideally meet during a clean turn?
options: At the centre of the front axle between the steering arms
At the steering column where the pinion meets the rack
At a single turn centre on the extension of the rear axle line
At the vehicle's centre of gravity above the floor pan
questions.explain: Each wheel's axis must pass through a common turn centre located on the extension of the rear axle line.
questions.src: located on the extension of the rear axle line

questions.q: How does Ackermann geometry produce the unequal steering angles mechanically?
options: A hydraulic valve that delays steering of the outer front wheel
Angled steering arms whose projected lines meet near the rear axle centre
A rack with unequal tooth pitch on its left and right halves
Different tyre sizes fitted to the left and right front wheels
questions.explain: The steering arms are angled inward so their projected lines meet close to the centre of the rear axle.
questions.src: angling the steering arms inward

questions.q: Which alignment term is the inward or outward tilt of the wheel from vertical, viewed from the front?
options: Camber
Toe
Scrub radius
Caster
questions.explain: Caster is the rearward tilt of the steering axis viewed from the side; toe is the inward or outward pointing of the wheel front.
questions.src: the inward or outward tilt of the wheel from vertical, viewed from the front

questions.q: Which alignment parameter makes the steering self-centre after a turn and adds stability at speed?
options: Negative camber
Positive camber
Toe-out
Positive caster
questions.explain: Positive caster works like the trailing pivot of a trolley caster wheel.
questions.src: Positive caster is what makes the steering self-centre

questions.q: Which alignment parameter is the most sensitive to a kerb strike?
options: Ride height
Camber
Toe
Caster
questions.explain: Toe governs straight-line stability and turn-in response, and is the parameter most sensitive to a kerb strike.
questions.src: the alignment parameter most sensitive to a kerb strike

questions.q: In a MacPherson strut layout, what serves as one of the suspension's locating members?
options: The anti-roll bar link
The strut tube itself
The steering tie rod
The upper wishbone
questions.explain: The damper doubles as the wheel's upper pivot, so only a lower control arm is needed to complete the linkage.
questions.src: the strut tube itself serves as one of the suspension's locating members

questions.q: What is the drawback of the MacPherson strut compared with double wishbone?
options: It cannot be fitted with a conventional coil spring
It needs more arms and takes up more packaging space
It adds more unsprung mass than a double wishbone
Camber gain is harder to control independently of ride height
questions.explain: Its compactness makes it dominant on transverse-engine vehicles, at the cost of harder-to-control camber gain.
questions.src: camber gain that is harder to control independently of ride height

questions.q: How does a double-wishbone suspension locate the wheel?
options: With two separate, roughly parallel arms, one above the other
With a single lower arm and the strut tube as the upper pivot
With one trailing arm per wheel and a torsion beam
With a solid beam axle located by a Panhard rod and trailing arms
questions.explain: Each arm pivots independently at the chassis and meets at the upright.
questions.src: locates the wheel with two separate, roughly parallel arms

questions.q: Why is double-wishbone geometry favoured where cornering performance matters most?
options: It places the spring and damper in a single load-bearing tube
It has the lowest part count and the simplest packaging
Camber and scrub can be tuned largely independently of spring travel
It is the lightest layout available, with the least unsprung mass
questions.explain: Varying the relative length and angle of the two arms lets camber and scrub be tuned independently.
questions.src: camber and scrub can be tuned largely independently of spring travel

questions.q: What is unsprung mass?
options: The weight of the body, passengers and luggage carried by the springs
Only the mass of the wheels and tyres, excluding brakes and linkage
Everything the spring does not support: wheel, tyre, brake and outboard linkage
The mass of the engine and transmission mounted on the subframe
questions.explain: Unsprung mass must accelerate up and down with every road irregularity independently of the body.
questions.src: Unsprung mass - everything the spring does not support

questions.q: What is the effect of reducing unsprung mass?
options: Ride and grip both improve at the same time
Grip improves, but the ride becomes harsher
Ride improves, but grip is reduced as a result
Only fuel consumption improves, not ride or grip
questions.explain: A lighter unsprung mass lets the tyre follow the road more closely, improving both rather than trading one against the other.
questions.src: improves both ride and grip simultaneously

questions.q: What does the strut's input flange connect the strut to?
options: The anti-roll bar link
The steering rack end
The strut top mount
The lower control arm
questions.explain: The input flange is for connecting the strut to the lower control arm; the output shaft is the wheel hub spindle.
questions.src: connection of the strut to the lower control arm

questions.q: What is the specification for front caster?

questions.src: Front caster | 3.5° ± 0.5°

questions.q: Which symptoms result when front toe is out of tolerance?
options: Inner-shoulder wear only
Feathered wear and unstable turn-in
Uneven tyre wear and a pull to one side
Wandering or heavy self-centring

questions.q: What is the rear camber specification?
questions.explain: Rear camber is -0.8° ± 0.3°; out of tolerance it causes inner-shoulder wear.
questions.src: Rear camber | -0.8° ± 0.3°

questions.q: What type of lubrication does the steering gear use?
options: A splash-type system for the rack and pinion
A pressure-fed oil circuit from the engine's pump
A wick-fed grease cup on each tie-rod end
A sealed dry-film coating that is never replenished
questions.explain: Grease in the housing is carried by the rotating pinion and distributed by splash.
questions.src: splash-type lubrication system

questions.q: How is the steering gear's grease level checked?
options: With a dipstick while the engine runs
By weighing the housing
By a sight glass, from ground level
By removing the pinion
questions.explain: The level is checked via a sight glass and can be verified from ground level.
questions.src: Grease level is checked via a sight glass

questions.q: At what temperature does the steering gear's temperature switch give a high-temperature warning?
options: Above 150 °C
Above 115 °C
Above 88 °C
Above 99 °C
questions.explain: The switch warns above 115 °C.
questions.src: high-temperature warning above 115 °C

questions.q: In the alignment procedure, what is adjusted first?
options: Toe, at both axles
Caster at the rear axle
Ride height at both axles
Camber at the front axle
questions.explain: Adjust toe first at both axles, then camber where the strut top-mount slots allow.
questions.src: Adjust toe first, at both axles, then camber

questions.q: What is the tightening torque for the tie-rod locknut?
options: 40 newton metres
110 newton metres
22 newton metres
55 newton metres
questions.explain: Tie-rod locknut 55 N-m; strut top-mount nuts 40 N-m - torqued once adjustment is confirmed.
questions.src: tie-rod locknut to 55 newton metres

questions.q: Why was 48 V chosen for the mild-hybrid second battery?
options: It sits just below the 60 V high-voltage threshold
It is the lowest voltage a lithium-ion cell can supply
It matches the rated voltage of the starter motor
It halves the weight of the 12 V wiring harness
questions.explain: Staying under 60 V allows much more power without the insulation, connector and training requirements of high-voltage EV systems.
questions.src: sits just below the 60 V threshold

questions.q: For the same current, roughly how much more power can a 48 V circuit carry than a 12 V circuit?
options: About eight times
About four times
The same
About twice
questions.explain: Power is voltage times current, so 48 V is roughly four times 12 V for the same current.
questions.src: roughly four times that of a 12 V circuit for the same current

questions.q: Before measuring open-circuit battery voltage, what must be done?
options: Disconnect the negative cable and wait five minutes
Connect a charger to the battery to stabilise the reading
Switch off all loads and rest the vehicle for 30 minutes or more
Run the engine at 2000 RPM with the headlamps switched on
questions.explain: A surface charge otherwise produces an optimistic reading.
questions.src: rested for at least 30 minutes

questions.q: An open-circuit reading of 12.4 V indicates roughly what state of charge?
options: 100 percent
50 percent
25 percent
75 percent
questions.explain: 12.6 V or above is fully charged, 12.4 V is about 75 percent, 12.2 V about 50 percent, and below 12.0 V is deeply discharged.
questions.src: 12.4 V - approximately 75 percent charged

questions.q: Between what values should charging voltage stabilise in the alternator output test (2000 RPM, no loads)?
questions.explain: Confirm charging voltage stabilises between 13.8 V and 14.6 V.
questions.src: between 13.8 V and 14.6 V

questions.q: With headlamps, blower at maximum and rear demister on, charging voltage should remain above what?
questions.explain: Under load the voltage must remain above 13.0 V.
questions.src: voltage remains above 13.0 V

questions.q: AC ripple above what value on the alternator's DC output indicates a failed rectifier diode?
options: 0.05 V AC
0.5 V AC
5 V AC
2 V AC
questions.explain: A reading above 0.5 V AC indicates a failed diode in the rectifier pack.
questions.src: A reading above 0.5 V AC indicates a failed diode

questions.q: An output that stays persistently above which value indicates a faulty voltage regulator?
questions.explain: Persistently above 15.0 V will damage the battery and connected electronics if left in service.
questions.src: persistently above 15.0 V indicates a faulty voltage regulator

questions.q: What is the maximum permissible voltage drop on the starter earth (negative) path?
questions.explain: The positive path may drop 0.5 V; the earth path only 0.2 V. Crank for no more than 10 seconds.
questions.src: maximum permissible drop on the earth path is 0.2 V

t0044.title: Ch 4 - 2. CAN-BUS NETWORKS & BODY CONTROL MODULE

questions.q: How do the vehicle's modules communicate?
options: Each broadcasts onto a shared twisted pair; others read what they need
A central ECU polls each module in turn and relays the replies
Each module transmits wirelessly to the gateway, which relays it
Each has a dedicated wire running to every module that needs it
questions.explain: A Controller Area Network replaces discrete wiring, reducing harness weight and letting one sensor reading serve many consumers.
questions.src: communicate over a Controller Area Network rather than discrete wiring

questions.q: How many physically separate CAN networks are fitted, and what bridges them?
options: Three, bridged by the BCM
One, with no bridge
Two, bridged by the ECU
Two, bridged by a gateway
questions.explain: A high-speed and a low-speed network, bridged by the gateway module.
questions.src: Two physically separate networks are fitted, bridged by a gateway

questions.q: What is the data rate of the high-speed CAN network?
options: 250 kilobits per second
500 kilobits per second
1000 kilobits per second
125 kilobits per second
questions.explain: High-speed CAN runs at 500 kbit/s and carries powertrain and chassis modules.
questions.src: High-speed CAN - 500 kilobits per second

questions.q: What is the data rate of the low-speed CAN network?
options: 50 kilobits per second
500 kilobits per second
125 kilobits per second
1000 kilobits per second
questions.explain: Low-speed CAN runs at 125 kbit/s and carries comfort and body functions.
questions.src: Low-speed CAN - 125 kilobits per second

questions.q: Which modules sit on the high-speed CAN network?
options: Door modules, seat controls and interior lighting
The BCM, seat controls and the ECU
The gateway and the Body Control Module
ECU, Transmission Control Module and ABS
questions.explain: Door, seat and lighting modules are comfort/body functions on the low-speed network.
questions.src: The ECU, Transmission Control Module (TCM) and ABS all sit on this network

questions.q: What resistance is measured across the high-speed CAN pair with the ignition off?
options: Approximately 120 ohms
Approximately 240 ohms
Approximately 60 ohms
Approximately 30 ohms
questions.explain: A 120 ohm terminating resistor sits at each end; the two in parallel measure about 60 ohms across the pair.
questions.src: giving approximately 60 Ω measured across the pair with the ignition off

questions.q: Which network is fault-tolerant and carries on operating on a single wire if the other is damaged?
options: Low-speed CAN
Neither network
High-speed CAN
Both networks
questions.explain: The low-speed network is fault-tolerant.
questions.src: It is fault-tolerant and continues operating on a single wire

questions.q: How does a failed gateway typically present?
options: As a steady excessive draw on the battery
As multiple modules reported unreachable at once
As a single module storing a communication DTC
As the BCM failing while everything else works
questions.explain: It should not be mistaken for several simultaneous module failures.
questions.src: presents as multiple modules reported as unreachable at once

questions.q: Which module is the busiest node on the low-speed network?
options: The Transmission Control Module (TCM)
The Engine Control Unit (ECU)
The diagnostic gateway module
The Body Control Module (BCM)
questions.explain: The BCM manages lighting, central locking, wipers and the immobiliser interface.
questions.src: It is the busiest node on the low-speed network

questions.q: How long may the vehicle take to enter sleep mode before a parasitic draw check?
options: Up to 15 minutes
Up to 5 minutes
Up to 45 minutes
Up to 2 hours
questions.explain: Close all doors, switch off all loads and allow up to 45 minutes on this model.
questions.src: may take up to 45 minutes on this model

questions.q: Why use a clamp meter where available for the parasitic draw check?
options: It reads the AC ripple on the battery posts directly
It avoids the need to disable the ignition system
It measures resistance more accurately than a multimeter
It avoids breaking the circuit, which could wake modules
questions.explain: An ammeter in series with the negative cable breaks the circuit, which may wake sleeping modules and restart the timer.
questions.src: breaking the circuit may wake sleeping modules and restart the timer

questions.q: What is the permissible maximum settled parasitic current?
options: 5 milliamps
50 milliamps
5 amps
500 milliamps
questions.explain: The permissible maximum is 50 mA.
questions.src: The permissible maximum is 50 milliamps

questions.q: If parasitic draw exceeds specification, how is the affected circuit isolated?
options: Pull fuses one at a time and watch the current each time
Measure the coil resistance of every relay in the vehicle
Disconnect the battery positive and retest after sleep mode
Replace the BCM and repeat the whole sleep-mode wait
questions.explain: The fuse whose removal drops the current identifies the circuit at fault.
questions.src: remove fuses one at a time and observe the current after each removal

questions.q: Removing a fuse to inspect it visually will reveal a cracked element that only fails under load.
options: True
False
questions.explain: It won't - test fuses in place using the exposed probe points while the circuit is energised.
questions.src: Removing a fuse to inspect it visually will not reveal a cracked element under load

questions.q: Battery voltage at only ONE of a fuse's two probe points indicates what?
options: A shorted fuse
A healthy fuse
A fault upstream of the fuse
An open fuse
questions.explain: Battery voltage at both points is healthy; at one point only means an open fuse; at neither means a fault upstream.
questions.src: Battery voltage at one point only indicates an open fuse

questions.q: No voltage at either probe point of a fuse indicates what?
options: A healthy fuse with a good supply on both sides
A cracked fuse element visible when removed
A fault upstream of the fuse, not in the fuse
An open fuse that must be replaced at once
questions.explain: The supply is missing before the fuse is reached.
questions.src: No voltage at either point indicates a fault upstream of the fuse

questions.q: What coil resistance should be measured across relay pins 85 and 86?
options: 60 Ω to 120 Ω
6 Ω to 12 Ω
0 Ω
questions.explain: An open circuit or a short indicates a failed coil.
questions.src: Expect 60 Ω to 120 Ω

questions.q: Which relay pin is the normally open output?
options: Pin 85
Pin 87
Pin 30
Pin 86
questions.explain: Continuity between pin 30 (common input) and pin 87 should appear only when the coil is energised.
questions.src: Pin 87 - normally open output

questions.q: Which three elements make up a torque converter?
options: A sun gear, a ring gear and a carrier
An impeller, a turbine and a stator
A pump, a valve body and a solenoid
A clutch plate, a flywheel and a release bearing
questions.explain: The impeller is driven by the engine, the turbine connects to the input shaft, and the stator redirects returning fluid.
questions.src: an impeller driven by the engine, a turbine connected to the input shaft, and a stator

questions.q: What torque multiplication does the converter reach at stall?
options: Approximately 1.0 to 1
Approximately 10 to 1
Approximately 2.2 to 1
Approximately 4.5 to 1
questions.explain: The stator multiplies torque at low speed, to about 2.2 to 1 at stall.
questions.src: approximately 2.2 to 1 at stall

questions.q: Above roughly what road speed does the lock-up clutch couple impeller and turbine?
options: 20 kilometres per hour
100 kilometres per hour
120 kilometres per hour
60 kilometres per hour
questions.explain: Locking up eliminates slip and improves fuel consumption.
questions.src: above roughly 60 kilometres per hour

questions.q: When does the TCM release converter lock-up?
options: During gear changes and under hard acceleration
Only when the vehicle is stationary
While cruising steadily at highway speed
Whenever the air conditioning is switched on
questions.explain: The TCM releases lock-up during gear changes and under hard acceleration.
questions.src: releases lock-up during gear changes and under hard acceleration

questions.q: What does a numerically higher gear ratio do?
options: Multiplies road speed but reduces the torque at the wheels
Multiplies torque but lowers road speed per engine revolution
Has no effect on torque, only on the synchroniser engagement
Reduces torque and road speed together at every engine speed
questions.explain: That is why first gear is the numerically highest ratio and top gear the lowest.
questions.src: a numerically higher gear ratio multiplies torque at the cost of road speed per engine revolution

questions.q: How is each ratio selected in a manual gearbox?
options: By sliding a synchroniser sleeve into engagement
By applying clutch packs through the valve body
By holding a planetary member stationary
By changing the final-drive ratio
questions.explain: Fixed pairs of meshing gears are selected by a synchroniser sleeve, not by changing which teeth are in mesh.
questions.src: selected by sliding a synchroniser sleeve into engagement

questions.q: Between what values is valve body line pressure regulated?
options: 10 bar at idle to 40 bar under full throttle
1 bar at idle to 5 bar under full throttle
4 bar at idle to 18 bar under full throttle
18 bar at idle to 4 bar under full throttle
questions.explain: Line pressure rises with throttle from 4 bar to 18 bar.
questions.src: between 4 bar at idle and 18 bar under full throttle

questions.q: Why does the TCM exchange torque and load data with the ECU during a shift?
options: So the torque converter can be bypassed at low speed
So fuel injection can be cut off for the whole shift
So the line pressure can be reset after each gear change
So ignition timing can be retarded briefly, smoothing the shift
questions.explain: The TCM also reports any DTC to the diagnostic system.
questions.src: so ignition timing can be momentarily retarded during a shift

questions.q: Which members make up a planetary gear set?
options: An input shaft, a synchroniser sleeve and a gear hub
A sun gear, a ring gear and planet gears on a carrier
A pinion, a rack and two tie rods on a steering arm
An impeller, a turbine and a stator in a fluid housing
questions.explain: Each set has a sun gear at the centre, an internally-toothed ring gear, and several planet gears carried on a common carrier.
questions.src: a sun gear at the centre, a ring gear surrounding it with internal teeth

questions.q: What do the planet gears mesh with?
options: Only the ring gear, never the sun gear
Only the carrier, which holds them in place
Both the sun gear and the ring gear
Only the sun gear, never the ring gear
questions.explain: Each planet gear meshes with both the sun and the ring simultaneously.
questions.src: each meshing with both the sun and the ring simultaneously

questions.q: How does a planetary set produce a distinct fixed ratio?
options: By sliding gears in and out of mesh with a sleeve
By changing the number of planet gears in mesh
By varying line pressure to change the gear diameters
By holding one member while driving another
questions.explain: Because sun, ring and carrier are always geared together, holding one while driving another fixes the ratio at the third.
questions.src: holding any one of them stationary while driving another produces a distinct fixed ratio at the third

questions.q: Why can an automatic transmission shift under load, unlike a manual gearbox with sliding-mesh synchronisers?
options: No gear ever leaves mesh in a planetary set
It uses a lower final-drive ratio than a manual box
It disconnects the engine completely during each shift
It uses a much larger clutch than a manual gearbox
questions.explain: The gears stay in mesh throughout; only which member is held or driven changes.
questions.src: without any gear ever leaving mesh

questions.q: In a reduction stage, which planetary member is typically the input?
options: The ring gear
The output shaft
The sun gear
The planet gears
questions.explain: The sun gear is the smallest member and is typically the input in a reduction stage.
questions.src: Sun gear - smallest member, typically the input in a reduction stage

questions.q: Which planetary member is commonly held for underdrive ratios?
options: The planet gears
The sun gear
The torque converter
The ring gear
questions.explain: The outer, internally-toothed ring gear is commonly held for underdrive ratios.
questions.src: commonly held for underdrive ratios

questions.q: If one wheel loses traction entirely on an open differential, what happens to the torque?
options: The gripping wheel takes all the torque; the spinning wheel gets none
Both wheels still receive half of the available torque each
The spinning wheel takes all the torque; the gripping wheel gets none
The differential locks automatically and drives both wheels equally
questions.explain: An open differential always splits torque equally between output shafts regardless of grip, so the wheel that loses traction absorbs all of it.
questions.src: that wheel absorbs all the available torque and the other, gripping wheel gets none

questions.q: What does a clutch-type limited-slip differential add?
options: A second ring gear that locks the two output shafts
A stack of friction clutch plates in the differential case
A hydraulic accumulator that boosts pressure to one wheel
A torque converter between the case and the output shafts
questions.explain: The plates sit between each output shaft and the differential case, and resist relative rotation between the two output shafts.
questions.src: adds a stack of friction clutch plates between each output shaft and the differential case

questions.q: How is the LSD clutch pack loaded?
options: Spring preload, plus ramps that react to input torque
Centrifugal weights that swing out as the wheels spin
The release bearing acting on a diaphragm spring
Line pressure supplied by the transmission valve body
questions.explain: The pack is preloaded by spring pressure and further compressed by ramps reacting to input torque.
questions.src: preloaded by spring pressure and further compressed by ramps that react to input torque

questions.q: What clamps the friction disc against the flywheel in a manual clutch?
options: Hydraulic pressure from the valve body
Centrifugal weights that swing out with engine speed
The release bearing acting on the flywheel
The diaphragm spring's own preload
questions.explain: The diaphragm-spring pressure plate clamps the disc using the spring's preload.
questions.src: clamps the friction disc against the flywheel using the spring's own preload

questions.q: What happens to the clamping force when the clutch pedal is depressed?
options: The synchroniser sleeve is released from the selected gear hub
The flywheel is mechanically disconnected from the crankshaft
The release bearing collapses the diaphragm spring's clamping force
The spring preload is doubled so the disc grips the flywheel harder
questions.explain: The release bearing pivots the diaphragm spring's fingers, and the disc slips free of the flywheel.
questions.src: collapsing the spring's clamping force and letting the disc slip free

questions.q: Why does clutch pedal feel change gradually rather than failing suddenly?
options: The flywheel gradually loses mass through repeated heating
The release bearing seizes up a little more each month
Hydraulic fluid slowly leaks from the clutch master cylinder
Clamping force falls as the spring wears and the disc thins
questions.explain: Pedal feel changes gradually over the disc's service life.
questions.src: pedal feel changes gradually over the disc's service life rather than failing suddenly

t0058.title: Ch 5 - 4. TCM VALVE BODY & DIAGNOSTIC PROCEDURES

questions.q: What does code P0700 mean?
options: Pressure control solenoid electrical fault
Transmission control system malfunction
Shift solenoid A electrical fault
Input shaft speed sensor circuit fault
questions.explain: P0700 is generic: always read the TCM directly for the specific underlying code.
questions.src: P0700 - Transmission control system malfunction

questions.q: What should you do after reading P0700?
options: Replace the valve body and repeat the road test
Replace the torque converter and flush the fluid
Read the TCM directly for the specific underlying code
Clear the code and monitor whether it returns

questions.q: Which code indicates an input shaft speed sensor circuit fault?

questions.q: What is frequently behind code P0740?

A failed battery or a loose earth strap
A worn clutch disc or a weak diaphragm spring
questions.explain: P0740 is a torque converter clutch circuit malfunction.

questions.q: What torque are the transmission pan bolts tightened to?

11 newton metres, in a circular sequence
35 newton metres, in a circular sequence
45 newton metres, in a diagonal sequence
questions.explain: Pan bolts: 12 N-m. (Fluid level plug 35, valve body bolts 11, converter-to-flexplate bolts 45.)
questions.src: tightening the pan bolts in a diagonal sequence to 12 newton metres

questions.q: What is the torque for the torque converter to flexplate bolts?
options: 35 newton metres
45 newton metres
11 newton metres
12 newton metres
questions.explain: Converter-to-flexplate bolts: 45 N-m.
questions.src: Torque converter to flexplate bolts | 45 newton metres

questions.q: What is the line pressure at idle in Drive?
options: 1 bar to 2 bar
18 bar
10 bar to 12 bar
4 bar to 5 bar
questions.explain: At full throttle it is 18 bar.
questions.src: Line pressure at idle (Drive) | 4 bar to 5 bar

questions.q: After refilling the transmission following solenoid replacement, what should be done?
options: Idle the engine for ten minutes and check for leaks only
Leave the stored codes in place for the next service visit
Clear stored codes, then road test through every forward ratio
Re-torque the pan bolts to 45 newton metres after a road test
questions.explain: Confirm correct operation through a road test covering every forward ratio.
questions.src: clear all stored codes, and confirm correct operation through a road test covering every forward ratio

questions.q: What cycle does cabin cooling run on?
options: The vapour-compression cycle
The ammonia absorption cycle
The Rankine steam cycle
The Otto thermodynamic cycle
questions.explain: A refrigerant is repeatedly compressed, condensed, expanded and evaporated in a closed loop.
questions.src: vapour-compression refrigeration cycle

questions.q: What makes it possible to move heat from the cabin to warmer outside air?
options: The heat absorbed by the expansion valve itself
The airflow the radiator fan pushes through the condenser
The work the compressor puts into the cycle
The pressure the expansion tank holds on the coolant
questions.explain: The result is made possible entirely by the work the compressor puts into the cycle.
questions.src: made possible entirely by the work the compressor puts into the cycle

questions.q: What regulates the engine cooling loop?
options: A condenser fan rather than a thermostat
A thermostat rather than a compressor
An expansion valve rather than a thermostat
A compressor rather than a thermostat
questions.explain: Engine cooling runs a separate loop using liquid coolant, regulated by a thermostat.
questions.src: regulated by a thermostat rather than a compressor

questions.q: Why has R1234yf superseded R134a on new vehicles?
options: R134a was found to deplete the ozone layer faster than R12
R1234yf is non-flammable, which makes it safer to service
R134a is no longer compatible with modern compressors
R134a's global-warming potential is far higher than R1234yf's
questions.explain: R134a has zero ozone-depletion potential, but its global-warming potential is roughly 1,430 times that of CO2, against roughly 4 for R1234yf.
questions.src: R134a's global-warming potential is roughly 1,430 times that of carbon dioxide, against roughly 4 for R1234yf

questions.q: Why are R1234yf service equipment, fittings and labels deliberately incompatible with R134a equipment?
options: R134a is flammable, so its fittings are specially sealed
R1234yf is mildly flammable, and mixing the two is prohibited
R1234yf runs at far higher pressures than R134a does
R1234yf is toxic to touch, so it needs sealed fittings
questions.explain: The two refrigerants must never be mixed in one system.
questions.src: the two must never be mixed in one system

questions.q: What does the compressor do?
options: Compresses low-pressure vapour, raising its pressure and temperature
Cools the high-pressure vapour until it condenses into a liquid
Meters the high-pressure liquid through a fixed restriction
Absorbs heat from the cabin air passing over its fins
questions.explain: It raises the refrigerant well above ambient pressure and temperature.
questions.src: draws in low-pressure refrigerant vapour and compresses it

questions.q: What happens in the condenser?
options: Drops the liquid's pressure sharply through a small restriction
Cools the passing cabin air by absorbing heat from it
Boils low-pressure liquid back into vapour inside the cabin
Rejects heat to outside air as the vapour condenses to liquid
questions.explain: The hot, high-pressure vapour rejects heat to the outside air and condenses to a high-pressure liquid.
questions.src: rejects heat to the outside air as the hot, high-pressure vapour condenses

questions.q: Where is the condenser mounted?
options: Inside the HVAC housing beside the blower motor
Ahead of the radiator in the airflow
Behind the evaporator in the cabin air duct
Mounted on the compressor shaft pulley
questions.explain: It is mounted ahead of the radiator in the airflow.
questions.src: mounted ahead of the radiator in the airflow

questions.q: What does the expansion valve do?
options: Rejects the refrigerant's heat to the outside airflow
Absorbs heat from cabin air as the refrigerant boils
Meters high-pressure liquid through a restriction, dropping its pressure
Compresses low-pressure vapour, raising its pressure and temperature
questions.explain: Part of the liquid flash-evaporates, cooling the rest dramatically before it reaches the evaporator.
questions.src: meters the high-pressure liquid through a restriction

questions.q: What does the evaporator do?
options: Stores the refrigerant charge and removes any moisture
Absorbs cabin heat, boiling the refrigerant back into low-pressure vapour
Compresses the vapour so that it reaches the condenser hot
Rejects the absorbed heat to the air passing over its fins
questions.explain: It sits inside the HVAC housing; the vapour then returns to the compressor to repeat the cycle.
questions.src: absorbs heat from cabin air passing over its fins

questions.q: In which order does refrigerant pass through the four main components?
options: Compressor, evaporator, expansion valve, condenser
Condenser, compressor, evaporator, expansion valve
Expansion valve, compressor, condenser, evaporator
Compressor, condenser, expansion valve, evaporator
questions.explain: The cycle repeats: compress, condense, expand, evaporate.
questions.src: Evaporator - inside the HVAC housing

questions.q: Which part of the loop is the 'low side'?
options: The cold, low-pressure refrigerant at the evaporator
The hot, high-pressure gas leaving the compressor
The liquid condensing inside the condenser coil
The high-pressure liquid arriving at the expansion valve
questions.explain: The low side is cold, low-pressure refrigerant absorbing cabin heat through the evaporator; the high side is hot high-pressure refrigerant through the condenser.
questions.src: Low side - cold low-pressure refrigerant absorbing cabin heat through the evaporator

questions.q: What coolant mixture circulates through the engine?

Water and mineral oil
Pure distilled water
Water and methyl alcohol

questions.q: What allows the cooling system to run above 100 °C without boiling?

The wax-pellet thermostat valve
A pressurised expansion tank
The electric radiator cooling fan

questions.q: What type of valve is the thermostat?

A vacuum diaphragm valve
A wax-pellet valve

questions.q: While the thermostat is closed, where does the coolant flow?

It flows through the heater matrix only and the cabin vents
It flows through the radiator only, then back to the pump

questions.q: At about what temperature does the thermostat typically begin to open?
