questions.src: typically 88 °C

questions.q: What does the ECU use to command the electric radiator fan?
options: Engine oil pressure, measured at the main gallery
Vehicle road speed, measured at the wheel speed sensors
Cabin temperature, measured at the evaporator outlet
Coolant temperature, and A/C refrigerant high-side pressure
questions.explain: The fan runs whenever either circuit needs the airflow, independent of vehicle road speed.
questions.src: from coolant temperature and, on air-conditioned vehicles, from refrigerant high-side pressure as well

questions.q: The radiator fan only runs when the vehicle is moving.
options: True
False
questions.explain: The fan runs whenever either circuit needs airflow, independent of vehicle road speed.
questions.src: independent of vehicle road speed

questions.q: For how long must the system be evacuated under vacuum, at a minimum?
options: 30 minutes
10 minutes
5 minutes
60 minutes
questions.explain: Then confirm the vacuum holds for 5 minutes with the pump isolated.
questions.src: Evacuate the system under vacuum for a minimum of 30 minutes

questions.q: How long must the vacuum hold with the pump isolated, to prove there is no leak?
options: 15 minutes
1 minute
5 minutes
30 minutes
questions.explain: A rising pressure would mean air is leaking back in.
questions.src: vacuum holds for 5 minutes

questions.q: What is the effect of overcharging the refrigerant?
options: It improves cooling because more refrigerant absorbs more heat
It raises head pressure and reduces cooling performance
It has no effect once the charge exceeds the specified mass
It lowers head pressure but shortens compressor life
questions.explain: Overcharging reduces cooling as surely as undercharging does.
questions.src: overcharging raises head pressure and reduces cooling performance

questions.q: What low-side pressure is expected at idle in 25 °C ambient?
options: 50 kPa to 100 kPa
1200 kPa to 1600 kPa
350 kPa to 400 kPa
180 kPa to 250 kPa
questions.explain: The high side is 1200 kPa to 1600 kPa.
questions.src: Low-side pressure (idle, 25 °C ambient) | 180 kPa to 250 kPa

questions.q: What high-side pressure is expected at idle in 25 °C ambient?
options: 180 kPa to 250 kPa
1200 kPa to 1600 kPa
3000 kPa to 3500 kPa
350 kPa to 400 kPa
questions.explain: High-side 1200-1600 kPa; low-side 180-250 kPa.
questions.src: High-side pressure (idle, 25 °C ambient) | 1200 kPa to 1600 kPa

questions.q: At what point does the cooling fan switch on?
options: 1600 kPa low side
88 °C coolant, or 1200 kPa refrigerant high side
105 °C coolant only
99 °C coolant, or 1600 kPa refrigerant high side
questions.explain: 88 °C is the thermostat opening temperature, a different threshold.
questions.src: Cooling fan on-threshold | 99 °C coolant, or 1600 kPa refrigerant high side

questions.q: What recovery equipment may be used for refrigerant recovery?
options: Any recovery machine, since the connectors are universal
Only an R134a machine, whatever refrigerant is fitted
Only one identified for the refrigerant type in the vehicle
A vacuum pump with a gauge set, without a recovery machine
questions.explain: The two refrigerants must never be mixed.
questions.src: Use only a recovery machine identified for the refrigerant type fitted to the vehicle

questions.q: Where does a vehicle's mass shift when it accelerates, brakes or corners?
options: Always toward the centre line of the vehicle's wheelbase
Toward the end or side resisting the change in motion
Evenly across all four tyres, whatever the manoeuvre
Always toward the rear axle, whatever the manoeuvre
questions.explain: The mass does not press on all four tyres equally the instant the motion changes.
questions.src: it shifts, dynamically, toward whichever end or side is resisting the change in motion

questions.q: What does the traction circle represent?
options: The path a tyre follows when steered through a roundabout
The maximum steering angle available at the front wheels
The size of the contact patch at the rated tyre pressure
A tyre's one finite budget of grip, shared by all manoeuvres
questions.explain: Any combination of braking and cornering force is a point inside the circle.
questions.src: braking, accelerating or cornering all draw on the same finite budget of grip

questions.q: According to the traction circle, what does heavy braking leave little grip for?
options: Cornering
Steering lock
Accelerating
Straight-line travel
questions.explain: Heavy braking uses up the grip budget; heavy cornering leaves little for braking.
questions.src: heavy braking leaves little grip left over for cornering

questions.q: Why is trail-braking into a corner a skill rather than a free action?
options: It always locks the rear wheels before the front wheels
ABS switches itself off whenever the wheel is steered
Braking and cornering force draw on the same limited grip
The brakes cannot be applied while the wheel is turned
questions.explain: Combining both forces risks exceeding the circle.
questions.src: which is precisely why trail-braking into a corner is a skill rather than a free action

questions.q: A tyre can generate unlimited force provided the force acts in one direction only.
options: True
False
questions.explain: A contact patch generates only a limited total force before it breaks loose, regardless of the direction it acts in.
questions.src: can generate only a limited total force before it breaks loose, regardless of the direction

t0076.title: Ch 7 - 2. WEIGHT TRANSFER & BRAKING FORCE DISTRIBUTION

questions.q: Under braking, which axle gains load?
options: The front axle - the rear axle is unloaded
Neither axle changes load; only the tyres do
Both axles gain load equally under braking
The rear axle - the front axle is unloaded
questions.explain: Braking force at the tyres and inertia at the centre of gravity form a couple that unloads the rear axle and adds that load to the front.
questions.src: unloads the rear axle and adds that same load to the front

questions.q: What increases the amount of load transferred forward under braking?
options: A wider track and a stiffer anti-roll bar
A longer wheelbase and a lower ride height
A lower centre of gravity and gentler deceleration
A higher centre of gravity and harder deceleration
questions.explain: The higher the centre of gravity and the harder the deceleration, the more load transfers forward.
questions.src: The higher the centre of gravity and the harder the deceleration, the more load transfers forward

questions.q: A tall vehicle braking hard can, in the extreme, have its rear axle become the first to lock up despite carrying less of the static weight.
options: True
False
questions.explain: Enough load can transfer forward to unload the rear axle so much that it locks first.
questions.src: a taller vehicle braking hard can, in the extreme, unload the rear axle enough to make it the first to reach lock-up

questions.q: What does Electronic Brakeforce Distribution (EBD) do?
options: Raises rear-circuit pressure above front to use the rear grip
Cuts engine torque to reduce the load on the front axle
Trims rear-circuit pressure below front in proportion to load transfer
Splits brake pressure evenly between front and rear circuits
questions.explain: EBD works through the same ABS hydraulic control unit.
questions.src: continuously trims rear-circuit pressure below the front circuit's own pressure

questions.q: Why would splitting brake pressure evenly front and rear be a problem?
options: The vacuum servo would lose boost during every hard stop
The lightly-loaded rear wheels would lock before the front grip is used
The front wheels would lock well before the rears, losing steering
The HCU would overheat from constant pressure cycling in the pump
questions.explain: The front axle gains load and the rear loses it under braking.
questions.src: would lock the lightly-loaded rear wheels well before the front tyres' grip is fully used

questions.q: What input does EBD use to estimate load transfer?
options: The steering angle and yaw rate only
Signals from all four wheel speed sensors
The accelerator pedal position and engine torque
A load cell fitted to each axle beam
questions.explain: It trims rear pressure from the load transfer estimated from all four wheel speed sensors.
questions.src: estimated from all four wheel speed sensors

questions.q: Slip ratio compares what?
options: Front axle load against rear axle load, as a percentage of weight
Brake line pressure against pedal force, as a percentage of travel
Engine speed against wheel speed, as a percentage of redline
A wheel's actual speed against its free-rolling speed, as a percentage
questions.explain: A fully locked wheel is 100 percent slip.
questions.src: Slip ratio compares a wheel's actual rotational speed with the road speed it would have if rolling freely

questions.q: At what slip ratio is peak longitudinal grip typically produced for a road tyre on dry asphalt?
options: 10 percent to 20 percent
0 percent to 5 percent
40 percent to 50 percent
90 percent to 100 percent
questions.explain: A small amount of controlled slip lets the rubber shear and interlock with the road; beyond the peak grip falls, which is the point ABS exists to avoid.
questions.src: typically 10 percent to 20 percent for a road tyre on dry asphalt

questions.q: Why does lateral load transfer reduce an axle's total available grip?
options: The brakes drag on the outside wheels in a corner
Tyre pressure falls sharply as the car corners hard
Grip grows more slowly than load once load is high
The inside tyres gain load faster than the outside tyres
questions.explain: The outside tyres gain load and the inside tyres lose it, producing a net loss of grip.
questions.src: grip grows more slowly than load once load is high

questions.q: Which two changes can improve cornering grip without changing tyre size?
options: Lower tyre pressures and a softer spring
A wider track and a stiffer anti-roll bar
A narrower track and a softer anti-roll bar
A higher centre of gravity and a longer wheelbase
questions.explain: Both reduce the lateral load transfer penalty.
questions.src: a wider track and a stiffer anti-roll bar can measurably improve cornering grip

questions.q: What is understeer?
options: The front axle reaches its grip limit before the rear
The steering wheel becomes too light for the road speed
The rear axle reaches its grip limit before the front
Both axles reach their grip limit at the same moment
questions.explain: The vehicle follows a wider arc than the steering angle commands.
questions.src: the front axle reaches its grip limit before the rear

questions.q: What is the standard correction for understeer?
options: Accelerate to load the front tyres harder
Brake hard while turning the wheel sharply
Apply more steering lock to tighten the line
Reduce speed and unwind some steering lock
questions.explain: That lets the front tyres regain grip.
questions.src: reduce speed and unwind some steering lock

questions.q: What is the correction for oversteer?
options: Accelerate sharply to bring the rear back into line
Steer away from the slide and brake hard on the rears
Apply the handbrake to hold the rear wheels still
Steer into the slide promptly and ease off the rear load
questions.explain: The rear of the vehicle is rotating faster than the intended line.
questions.src: correction is steering input in the direction of the slide, applied promptly

questions.q: Why are most production vehicles tuned toward mild understeer at the limit?
options: It gives shorter stopping distances at the limit of grip
It wears the front and rear tyres more evenly
It is more predictable and easier for an average driver to correct
It lets the vehicle use a smaller and cheaper steering rack
questions.explain: Oversteer is the harder failure mode to recover from.
questions.src: it is the more predictable and more easily corrected of the two failure modes for an average driver

questions.q: What minimum deceleration must be achieved in the straight-line deceleration test?
options: 5.0 metres per second squared
2.5 metres per second squared
9.8 metres per second squared
7.5 metres per second squared
questions.explain: Confirm it meets or exceeds 7.5 m/s2 and that the vehicle tracks straight.
questions.src: meets or exceeds 7.5 metres per second squared

questions.q: Where may the straight-line deceleration test be performed?
options: On a downhill gradient to load the front axle
On any quiet public road at the test speed
Only on a closed, dry, level test surface
On a wet surface so that ABS intervenes
questions.explain: It must be done on a closed, dry, level test surface.
questions.src: Perform only on a closed, dry, level test surface

questions.q: What instrument records deceleration in the straight-line test?
options: A calibrated accelerometer
A tyre tread depth gauge on each wheel
A brake pressure gauge on each wheel
A multimeter clamped on the battery cable
questions.explain: Maximum brake pressure is applied without inducing ABS intervention.
questions.src: Record deceleration using a calibrated accelerometer

questions.q: What is the brake balance test performed on?
options: A chassis dynamometer
A roller brake tester
A skid pad
A wheel alignment rack
questions.explain: Each axle is run in turn and the peak braking force at each wheel recorded.
questions.src: Performed on a roller brake tester

questions.q: What is the maximum side-to-side braking imbalance at any one axle?
options: 50 percent of the higher reading
15 percent of the higher reading
30 percent of the higher reading
5 percent of the higher reading
questions.explain: Larger imbalance means a pull to one side under braking.
questions.src: does not exceed 15 percent of the higher reading

questions.q: What share of total braking force should the front axle contribute?
options: 45 percent to 55 percent
30 percent to 40 percent
80 percent to 90 percent
60 percent to 70 percent
questions.explain: This is consistent with the static and dynamic load split.
questions.src: 60 percent to 70 percent of total braking force

questions.q: What is the typical total voltage of a traction battery pack?
options: 12 V to 48 V
300 V to 800 V
60 V to 100 V
questions.explain: Cells are grouped into modules and modules into a pack, typically totalling 300 V to 800 V.
questions.src: typically totalling 300 V to 800 V depending on architecture

questions.q: Why is NMC chemistry chosen?
options: High energy density, so longer range per kilogram
Good performance at very low ambient temperatures
A greater tolerance of full charging and thermal abuse
The lowest cost per kilowatt-hour of any chemistry
questions.explain: NMC is Nickel Manganese Cobalt Oxide.
questions.src: chosen for its high energy density and therefore longer range per kilogram

questions.q: Why is LFP (Lithium Iron Phosphate) chemistry chosen?
options: The lowest pack weight of any lithium-ion chemistry
No need for any battery management system in the pack
The highest energy density, giving the longest range per kilogram
Tolerance of full charging and thermal abuse, with lower energy density
questions.explain: That trade-off is the main difference from NMC.
questions.src: greater tolerance of full charging and thermal abuse

questions.q: What does the Battery Management System (BMS) do if any cell strays outside safe voltage or temperature limits?
options: Switches the inverter into regenerative braking mode
Reduces the 12 V auxiliary supply to protect the pack
Immediately disconnects the pack's main contactors
Increases the charging current to rebalance the cells
questions.explain: It measures every cell group's voltage and the pack's temperature at multiple points.
questions.src: disconnecting the pack's own main contactors immediately

questions.q: Why does the BMS balance individual cells against one another?
options: To raise the pack voltage above its nominal rating
So the weakest cell does not limit the pack's usable capacity
To shorten the time the pack takes to fully charge
To keep the pack cool evenly during fast charging
questions.explain: Balancing keeps the pack's usable capacity from being set by its weakest cell.
questions.src: so the weakest cell does not limit the usable capacity of the whole pack

questions.q: What does the inverter convert?
options: Battery DC to three-phase AC (and the reverse in regeneration)
12 V DC to 48 V DC for the mild-hybrid starter
Three-phase AC to single-phase AC for the cabin
External mains AC to DC for charging the traction pack
questions.explain: During regenerative braking the process runs in reverse.
questions.src: converts the battery's DC supply into the three-phase AC waveform

questions.q: Which switching devices are increasingly replacing older IGBTs for lower switching losses?
options: Mechanical contactor relays
Silicon Carbide (SiC) devices
Gallium arsenide thyristors
Germanium bipolar transistors
questions.explain: SiC devices switch with lower losses.
questions.src: increasingly Silicon Carbide (SiC) devices rather than older IGBTs

questions.q: How does the inverter synthesise a smooth sine wave from a DC source?
options: By passing the DC through a large step-up transformer
By varying the battery voltage up and down smoothly
By rectifying the motor's back-EMF with a diode bridge
By varying each switch's on-time (pulse-width modulation)
questions.explain: Power transistors switch many thousands of times per second.
questions.src: by varying each switch's on-time (pulse-width modulation)

questions.q: What does PMSM stand for?
options: Permanent Magnet Series Motor
Pulse Modulated Switched Motor
Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor
Primary Magnet Stator Module
questions.explain: It is the most common traction motor type.
questions.src: A Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor (PMSM)

questions.q: How does a PMSM rotor turn relative to the inverter's rotating field?
options: In exact synchronism with the field, with no slip
Independently of the field, under its own inertia
At twice the speed of the field, as a gear stage
Slightly slower than the field, because of slip
questions.explain: Permanent magnets in the rotor lock onto the rotating field, unlike an induction motor's rotor which slips behind it.
questions.src: the rotor turns in exact synchronism with that field rather than slipping behind it

questions.q: What does the DC-DC converter do?
options: Converts battery DC into three-phase AC for the motor
Charges the traction battery from the mains supply
Balances the voltage of individual cell groups
Steps the HV down to feed the 12 V auxiliary system
questions.explain: The on-board charger, in contrast, converts external AC supply to DC for the pack.
questions.src: DC-DC converter - steps HV down to feed the 12 V auxiliary system

questions.q: What does the on-board charger do?
options: Steps the pack voltage down to feed the 12 V system
Converts the external AC supply to DC for the pack
Converts battery DC into three-phase AC for the motor
Drives the reduction gear through a clutch pack
questions.explain: The DC-DC converter feeds the 12 V system.
questions.src: On-board charger - converts external AC supply to DC for the pack

questions.q: What colour is high-voltage cable sheathing by convention?
options: Blue
Yellow
Orange
Red
questions.explain: Orange sheathing is used on every real vehicle.
questions.src: orange sheath, by convention

questions.q: What does the traction motor do when it acts as a generator during regenerative braking?
options: Charges only the 12 V battery through the DC-DC converter
Drives the pack cooling fan with the recovered energy
Turns kinetic energy back into electrical energy stored in the pack
Dissipates the kinetic energy as heat at the friction brakes
questions.explain: Energy is stored rather than dissipated as heat at the friction brakes.
questions.src: converting the vehicle's kinetic energy back into electrical energy stored in the pack

questions.q: What does the blending controller do?
options: Splits requested deceleration between regenerative and friction braking
Controls only the ABS inlet and outlet valves in each wheel circuit
Switches regeneration off permanently once the pack passes 50 percent
Balances the voltage of the individual cell groups in the pack
questions.explain: It hands off smoothly to the friction brakes at low speed or when the pack can't accept more charge.
questions.src: A blending controller apportions the driver's total requested deceleration

questions.q: When does braking hand off to the friction brakes?
options: Never - regeneration alone handles all the braking
As speed nears zero, or the pack's charge limit is reached
Only when the ABS activates on a slippery surface
Only once the pack has been completely discharged
questions.explain: A motor can no longer generate effectively near zero speed.
questions.src: as vehicle speed falls toward zero

questions.q: Regenerative braking applies its torque at which axle?
options: Both axles equally
The front axle always
The undriven axle
Only the driven axle
questions.explain: So it must be reduced or removed within milliseconds if that axle approaches lock.
questions.src: applies its torque only at the driven axle

questions.q: What happens to regenerative torque the instant the driven axle approaches wheel lock?
options: The pack contactors open and the 12 V system shuts down
It is held constant while the ABS cycles the valves
It is increased to slow the locking wheel more quickly
It is cut within milliseconds; the friction brakes and ABS take over
questions.explain: The same integrated braking system that manages EBD coordinates this, so the driver feels one blended pedal response.
questions.src: must be reduced or removed within milliseconds

questions.q: What is a High-Voltage Interlock Loop (HVIL)?
options: A low-voltage sense wire looped through every HV connector and cover
A relay that connects the 12 V battery to the contactors
A resistor that bleeds the drive capacitors after shutdown
A fuse that protects the high-voltage cabling from overload
questions.explain: Opening any one of them breaks the loop.
questions.src: A low-voltage sense wire is looped through every high-voltage connector

questions.q: What happens when the HVIL loop is broken?
options: A warning lamp lights, but the contactors stay closed
The 12 V battery is automatically disconnected from the chassis
The inverter is switched into regeneration to drain the pack
The BMS opens the main pack contactors within milliseconds
questions.explain: That is before a technician's hands can reach the exposed high-voltage contacts.
questions.src: the BMS opens the main pack contactors within milliseconds of detecting that break

questions.q: In the service disconnect procedure, which terminal is removed first from the 12 V battery?
options: Both terminals together, to avoid a voltage spike
Neither - the 12 V battery stays connected throughout
The negative terminal, isolating the contactor control circuit
The positive terminal, isolating the starter feed circuit
questions.explain: Remove the low-voltage 12 V battery's negative terminal first.
questions.src: Remove the low-voltage 12 V battery's negative terminal first

questions.q: What does removing the high-voltage service plug do?
options: Isolates only the 12 V auxiliary system from the pack
Physically opens the pack's main circuit, independent of contactors
Resets the BMS and clears all of its stored fault codes
Discharges the drive capacitors to zero volts instantly
questions.explain: It is a mechanical break, independent of contactor control.
questions.src: which physically opens the pack's main circuit independently of the contactors

questions.q: What is the typical wait for the drive system's capacitors to bleed down?
options: 1 to 2 minutes
5 to 10 minutes
45 to 60 minutes
30 to 60 seconds
questions.explain: Wait the manufacturer-specified discharge time.
questions.src: typically 5 to 10 minutes

questions.q: Before touching any orange-sheathed cable or connector, what must be done?
options: Check that the 12 V battery voltage has dropped to zero
Check that the HVIL warning lamp has gone out
Wait one further minute after removing the service plug
Confirm zero voltage at the HV connectors with a rated meter
questions.explain: Never assume it is safe.
questions.src: Confirm zero voltage directly at the high-voltage connectors using a rated meter

questions.q: What is the minimum PPE rating for high-voltage service?
options: Ordinary workshop gloves once the plug is removed
500 V insulated gloves only
1000 V insulated gloves and tools
100 V insulated gloves and tools
questions.explain: PPE rated for the system voltage is mandatory before beginning.
questions.src: Minimum PPE rating | 1000 V insulated gloves and tools

questions.q: The capacitor discharge threshold before service is below what voltage?
options: 60 V DC
12 V DC
120 V DC
300 V DC
questions.explain: Below 60 V DC.
questions.src: Capacitor discharge threshold before service | Below 60 V DC

questions.q: Which two construction philosophies does the manual describe?
options: The tubular spaceframe and the beam-axle chassis
The ladder-frame chassis and the unitised monocoque
The leaf-sprung and the coil-sprung chassis
The subframe cradle and the strut-tower chassis
questions.explain: Both remain in use.
questions.src: the body-on-frame ladder chassis, and the unitised monocoque

questions.q: How does a ladder frame carry structural loads?
options: Through the roof, pillars and sills of a welded shell
Through the engine block and the transmission casing
Through the floor pan alone, with no separate frame
Through two full-length steel rails joined by cross-members
questions.explain: The body sits on top through isolating bushes as a largely non-structural shell.
questions.src: carries every structural load through two full-length steel rails

questions.q: Why does the ladder frame persist on trucks and body-on-frame SUVs?
options: It gives the highest torsional stiffness for the weight
It is the cheapest layout to crash-test and certify
It suits body-swap flexibility and off-road twisting loads
It is the lightest layout available for a given stiffness
questions.explain: It absorbs severe off-road twisting loads without transmitting them into the cabin.
questions.src: absorbing severe off-road twisting loads without transmitting them into the cabin

questions.q: What is a monocoque?
options: One continuous welded shell that is itself the primary structure
A body mounted on two full-length rails through bushes
A tubular spaceframe clad in non-structural panels
A removable subframe carrying the engine and suspension
questions.explain: There is no separate frame underneath.
questions.src: there is no separate frame underneath

questions.q: What is the trade-off of monocoque construction compared with a ladder frame?
options: There is no trade-off between monocoque and ladder frame
Cheaper to build, but noticeably less stiff overall
Lighter for a given stiffness, but less off-road articulation
Heavier, but more tolerant of off-road twisting loads
questions.explain: That is why monocoque dominates passenger cars and crossovers.
questions.src: at the cost of the off-road articulation tolerance a ladder frame provides

questions.q: What is the purpose of crumple zones?
options: To stiffen the passenger cell against intrusion
To turn kinetic energy into controlled structural deformation
To make the front and rear of the vehicle lighter
To reduce noise and vibration reaching the cabin
questions.explain: The structure ahead of and behind the passenger cell deforms in a controlled, progressive sequence, rather than passing the energy into the occupants.
questions.src: converting the vehicle's kinetic energy into structural deformation work

questions.q: How are the location and sequence of rail folding controlled?
options: Rubber bushes fitted at the rail ends
Shear bolts that snap on first impact
Beads or notches pressed into the rail
Spring-loaded rail ends that retract
questions.explain: These crush initiators keep the collapse force within a controlled band rather than buckling unpredictably.
questions.src: crush initiators - beads or notches pressed into the rail

questions.q: In contrast to the crumple zones, how is the passenger cell engineered?
options: To resist deformation and keep the survival space intact
To absorb as much road and wind noise as it can
To crush progressively in the same way as the rails
To be as light as possible to cut fuel consumption
questions.explain: It uses higher-strength steel sections.
questions.src: the passenger cell itself is engineered to resist deformation

questions.q: Where are higher-strength steel sections used in the safety cage?
options: The floor pan, bulkhead and boot floor panels
The bonnet, doors and boot lid outer skins
The front and rear longitudinal rails and bumper beams
The A, B and C pillars, the sills and the roof rails
questions.explain: The crumple zones use crush initiators instead.
questions.src: at the A, B and C pillars, the sills and the roof rails

questions.q: The boundary between a crush zone and the resisting passenger cell is an incidental result of the body design.
options: True
False
questions.explain: It is a deliberately engineered structural boundary, not an incidental one.
questions.src: a deliberately engineered structural boundary, not an incidental one

questions.q: What does torsional stiffness describe?
options: Resistance of the roof pillars to crushing in a rollover
How much the structure twists, front relative to rear, under opposing loads
Resistance to sagging along the vehicle's length under its own weight
How far the crumple zones collapse in a frontal impact
questions.explain: Bending stiffness is the resistance to sagging along the vehicle's length.
questions.src: how much the structure twists, front relative to rear

questions.q: What does bending stiffness describe?
options: The stiffness of the tyre sidewalls under cornering load
How much the body twists, front relative to rear, under opposing loads
Resistance to sagging along the vehicle's length under its own weight
The combined stiffness of the springs and dampers
questions.explain: Torsional stiffness is the twisting stiffness.
questions.src: Bending stiffness describes resistance to sagging along the vehicle's length

questions.q: Why is stiffness a handling specification as well as a safety one?
options: A twisting body makes alignment under load less predictable than static
It alters the engine's power output at high road speed
It raises tyre pressures during hard cornering and braking
It directly changes the ratio of the steering rack and pinion
questions.explain: The twist absorbs some of the suspension's geometric changes.
questions.src: making the actual wheel alignment under load less predictable than the static alignment

questions.q: What does NVH stand for?
options: Noise, Velocity and Handling
Normal Vehicle Height
Negative Vibration Harmonics
Noise, Vibration and Harshness
questions.explain: NVH treatment absorbs energy the structure would otherwise carry to the occupants.
questions.src: Noise, Vibration and Harshness (NVH)

questions.q: What isolates powertrain vibration from the body?
options: Constrained-layer damping panels bonded to the floor
Sound-deadening material in the dash and wheel arches
Rubber and hydraulic engine and transmission mounts
Higher-strength steel in the A, B and C pillars
questions.explain: Damping panels and deadening material deal with panel vibration and airborne noise.
questions.src: Rubber and hydraulic engine and transmission mounts isolate powertrain vibration from the body

questions.q: How do constrained-layer damping panels work?
options: They turn panel vibration into a little heat in the damping layer
They absorb heat from the exhaust above the floor
They stiffen the panel to stop it vibrating at all
They reflect the sound back toward the road surface
questions.explain: They are bonded to large flat body sections.
questions.src: convert panel vibration into a small amount of heat within the damping layer itself

questions.q: What does sound-deadening material in the floor, dash and wheel arches attenuate?
options: Vibration from the engine mounts
Resonance of large body panels
Suspension movement over bumps
Airborne road and wind noise
questions.explain: It stops that noise reaching the cabin.
questions.src: attenuates airborne road and wind noise before it reaches the cabin

questions.q: How are body reference points checked after an impact?
options: By comparing with the opposite side of the body by eye
With a straight edge laid across the panel gaps
With a tape measure taken from the wheel centres out
Against dimensional data on a 3D measuring bench
questions.explain: Reference workcard MKMTM-39-10-00-210-3A.
questions.src: Measure body reference points against the manufacturer's dimensional data using a three-dimensional measuring bench

questions.q: What tolerance applies to body reference points?
options: ±0.3 mm from datum
±3 mm from datum
±30 mm from datum
±10 mm from datum
questions.explain: ±10 mm is the ADAS recalibration target distance tolerance, a different specification.
questions.src: Body reference point tolerance | ±3 mm from datum

questions.q: What evidence of prior deformation should be looked for in crush zones, even where the panel has been replaced?
options: Worn tread on the front tyre shoulders
A cracked windscreen near the pillar
